name: Autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy
aliases: autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant focal epilepsy classically linked to variants in neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit genes CHRNA4, CHRNB2 and CHRNA2, with additional cases from KCNT1 and DEPDC5
Seizures arise predominantly from sleep and consist of clusters of brief, stereotyped hypermotor events with dystonic or hyperkinetic posturing
Attacks are often abrupt, occur multiple times a night and may include vocalisation, thrashing or complex motor automatisms with preserved or rapidly recovered awareness
The nocturnal, stereotyped and clustering pattern frequently leads to misdiagnosis as a parasomnia or non-epileptic sleep disorder
Interictal and even ictal scalp EEG can be normal, so a normal EEG does not exclude the diagnosis
Video-EEG and polysomnography help distinguish these seizures from arousal parasomnias and REM behaviour disorder
KCNT1-related disease tends to be more severe and drug-resistant, sometimes with cognitive or psychiatric comorbidity
reference.pathophysiology: This disorder, now termed autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, is most often caused by gain-of-function variants in genes encoding subunits of the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CHRNA2), which alter cholinergic modulation of thalamocortical and frontal networks during sleep. Additional causes include KCNT1, encoding a sodium-activated potassium channel, and DEPDC5, part of the GATOR1 complex regulating the mTOR pathway. Abnormal excitability of frontal-lobe circuits during non-REM sleep generates the recurrent, brief, stereotyped hypermotor seizures, and the sleep-state dependence reflects the physiological modulation of these networks across the sleep-wake cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Non-REM arousal parasomnias (confusional arousals, sleep terrors, sleepwalking)
Other structural or genetic focal epilepsies
additionalInvestigations: Video-EEG monitoring to capture and characterise nocturnal events
Polysomnography to distinguish seizures from parasomnias and sleep disorders
Brain MRI to look for focal cortical dysplasia or other structural causes
Genetic testing including CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CHRNA2, KCNT1 and DEPDC5
Detailed sleep and family history with attack description from a bed partner
Home video recording of typical events
redFlags: Injuries sustained during violent nocturnal events
Daytime seizures or evolving neurological deficits suggesting a structural lesion
Drug-resistant seizures, particularly with KCNT1 variants
Cognitive or psychiatric decline requiring further evaluation
reference.prognosis: Seizures often persist through life but are typically well controlled with appropriate antiseizure medication, and cognition is usually preserved in the common receptor-subunit forms. KCNT1-related disease carries a less favourable outlook, being more often drug-resistant and associated with cognitive and behavioural difficulties.
pitfalls: Dismissing recurrent nocturnal events as parasomnias and delaying epilepsy diagnosis
Concluding that a normal scalp EEG excludes the condition
Failing to obtain video or polysomnographic evidence to characterise events
Not recognising that KCNT1-associated disease may need a different, targeted therapeutic approach
